speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: TRIBUTE ON NINETIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ORDER-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion of the ninetieth anniversary of the Victorian Order of Nurses, I would like to offer the Government of Canada's sincere congratulations to the Order, a national voluntary non-profit organization comprised of 75 branches in nine provinces across Canada.
It was in 1897, with the support of the National Council of Women, that Lady Aberdeen founded VON Canada. Lady Aberdeen had been actively promoting visiting nursing in Britain, where she had made the personal acquaintance of Florence Nightingale, who later wrote to her in Canada, and offered support and encouragement for the new Canadian nursing venture.
At a public meeting on February 10, 1897, Sir Wilfrid Laurier made a motion inaugurating the Order "as a mode of commemoration by the Dominion of the Queen's Diamond Jubilee". Lady Aberdeen was chosen president of the new Order, and on December 28 of the same year, Queen Victoria granted VON Canada a Royal Charter.
The Order's First 12 nurses were admitted at an official ceremony in November, 1897. After only five months, the Order organized a team of four nurses to accompany the Canadian Government Expedition to the Klondike. Throughout the 1917 Halifax disaster, the influenza epidemic of 1918, and two world wars, VON Canada continued to meet the challenging and changing needs of Canadians.
The first branches were organized in Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Halifax, Vancouver, and Kingston. When other requests for nursing services came from remote pioneer districts in the west, the VON offered to establish cottage hospitals. In 1898 the first of 44 cottage hospitals was opened in Regina. The last of these was turned over to local authorities in 1924.
More recently, in response to changing community needs, VON Canada is offering such innovative services as adult daycare, placement co-ordination, foot-care clinics, volunteer visiting, and such specialty services as palliative care and respiratory care.
During 1986, some 1,618 VON nurses provided more than three million home visits to 134,500 Canadians. I offer my thanks and congratulations, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all the Members in the House, to this active and vital organization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition I am pleased to join with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) this morning to honour the contribution of the Victorian Order of Nurses to Canadian health care on this, the occasion of its ninetieth anniversary.
The Minister has spoken this morning of the Order's first 90 years of service in Canada; of its selfless contribution in times of war, natural disaster and health epidemic. The mark of a truly great health organization is service to Canadians day in and day out in both urban and remote communities. The Victorian Order of Nurses meets and indeed surpasses this standard.
When, in the past, Canadians required nursing care, the Victorian Order of Nurses has always provided this public service with compassion, efficiency, and dedication. As Canadian society has changed and developed, so has the nursing services provided by the Victorian Order of Nurses. It is this ability to identify the needs of Canadians and to respond to those needs which will ensure that 90 years from now parliamentarians will again rise in the House to congratulate the Victorian Order of Nurses for its outstanding contribution to Canadian health care.

subtopic: TRIBUTE ON NINETIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ORDER-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me as health critic for the New Democratic Party to add our most sincere congratulations and appreciation to the Victorian Order of Nurses for 90 years of very special nursing services to Canadians.
The VON public health nurses and nurse practitioners have consistently pushed forward the frontiers of health care in Canada, bringing services to northern and remote communities and to the elderly and infirm in the comfort of their homes. They have a vision of a health care system which we as New Democrats share, a system that is preventive and community-based.
Many studies have shown that we must shift a much larger share of our health care dollars from curative to community care. Our population is rapidly aging and institutional care is very costly. It is essential that older people have the option to remain in their own homes as long as possible with a range of community support services like those provided so well by the VON.
1 am sure that VON nurses were pleased when Bill C-3, respecting the Canada Health Act, included a new Clause 9 to provide insurance coverage for "additional services rendered by health care practitioners". Unfortunately, to date no provinces have implemented this clause, which could greatly extend community nursing and paraprofessional services. The bulk of funding is still going to hospitals and nursing homes. Only 10 cents of the health care dollar goes to community support services.
1 call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to extend and expand the tradition established by the Victorian Order of Nurses by increasing funding for community nursing and by persuading provinces to implement Section 9 of the Canada Health Act.

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-OPPOSITION TO REMOVAL OF RURAL ROUTE SERVICE-WILNO, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a petition to present to the House of Commons on behalf of the rural communities in Canada which stand to lose their post offices over the next 10 years under this Government.
The Government has given direction to Canada Post to cut back on rural services and on rural post offices, whereby rural postmasters and postmistresses will be taken off salary, and we will not have a representative of Canada Post per se on the payroll of Canada Post in the rural communities of Canada.
The petitioners from Wilno, Ontario are a case in point. They feel that the fight for the Wilno Post Office is the fight for every rural community in Canada. They do not want to see these rural services diminished in any way, because the postmaster or postmistress is the one remaining public servant of Canada identified with the federal Government in many of those communities. He or she is well known to everybody in the community and stands as a representative of the federal Government of Canada and indeed a servant of the community.
Therefore, 1 present the petition to support their cause that the Government retain rural post offices for the services of rural communities.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are making history here today in the House of Commons but not the kind of history any of us could be proud of. Never before in this country, in this Parliament, has the House of Commons been asked to approve a legislative proposal not once, not twice but three times.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Three times we have been asked to pass a piece of legislation.
Let me recount very quickly the history of this legislation. All kinds of claims have been made as to its initiative, where it has come from, where it is tied to and so on. It bears reminding the House that in June, 1983 the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), then the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, introduced a White Paper on behalf of the Liberal Government which said in part:
To generate further growth in this industry-
Namely the pharmaceutical industry:
-the Government of Canada has decided to change the Patent Act to rebalance the 1969 policy.
That was the policy of the Liberal Government which needed to rebalance the 1969 changes to the Patent Act to generate growth in the pharmaceutical industry. On April 17, 1984 the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Judy Erola, appointed the Eastman Commission. In June, 1984, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), who at that point in time was duly elected and receiving briefings from Mr. Osbaldeston, continued to hold directorships of several companies, including the chairman of Sandoz Canada. In that capacity he was highly critical of compulsory licensing and said that it needed to be amended.
On July 16, 1984, during the election campaign, which deals with the question as to whether the Government has a mandate, the Progressive Conservative Party said:
A Progressive Conservative Government would review the Patent Act to ensure that intellectual capital is protected and to allow innovating companies to profit from the investment made in research and development without causing the consumer to pay unduly higher prices for medications.
We are on record as a Party during the election campaign as saying that we would change the Patent Act.
On February 16, 1985, four months after the Government was sworn in, the current Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Cote) then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, described the Government's intention to act on the pharmaceutical issue in a February 16 interview with Les Affaires, a Quebec business journal. The Minister stated that he intended to table a new policy for pharmaceuticals by the spring of 1985.
November 3, 1987

On February 22, 1985, again just four months after being sworn in, the Government, the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada and the Canadian Drug Manufacturers Association initialled a protocol suspending compulsory licensing applications while work proceeded concerning amendments to Section 41(4) of the Patent Act. Four months after the Government was elected, we had this protocol, but it came apart and was never acted upon. On February 28, 1985, the Eastman Commission reported. On March 15, the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs announced that consultations with the generic and brand name companies would be held. There were a series of consultations.
I might point out that on June 20, 1985, the then PQ Government of Quebec adopted a resolution unanimously in the National Assembly calling for amendments to the Patent Act. That was repeated by the newly elected Liberal Government of Quebec on December 19, 1985.
Someone has suggested that the trade negotiations were tied to Bill C-22. The Government in July, 1985 had P and P meetings in Baie Comeau. The Cabinet decision to initiate trade talks was announced in September, 1985. The amendments to the Patent Act came out of our commitment in the election and preceded by almost a year any concern about the decision respecting free trade.
One year ago on November 6, 1986, the Bill was finally given first reading in this Flouse. There were 12 hours of debate in this House and extensive committee hearings were held. Finally the Bill was sent to the Senate in May of this year. The Senate resisted all efforts on our side to encourage it to engage in pre-study on the Bill. That is something the Senate does quite often on complex and important Bills, but the Senate refused to do so in this instance. When the Bill was referred to the Senate, instead of giving it the usual treatment of reference to a standing committee, the Senate set up a special committee which went on a tour of the country to try to get some groundswell of opposition. Some $350,000 were spent on that. That committee reported at the end of June. I was around all the month of July making it known to the Senate that I was here to discuss the Bill with the Senators. I had only one meeting, and after prodding from our side finally, on August 12, the Senate reported. On August 26 this House discussed the motion to send the Bill back to the Senate.
I might mention a couple of quotes from the debates of that day. The Hon. Member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said:
-we believe the Senate should let the Bill pass after the House of Commons has, in fact, reviewed the matter.
On the same day the Leader of the Opposition, the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra, said:
Patent Act
-at the end of the day the elected House of Commons must prevail. That is
a clear position of the Liberal Party.
The Bill went back to the Senate. The Senate has then referred it to another committee. The Senators said they had no intention to delay, and I made it clear that 1 was anxious to appear before their committee. Finally, on October 3 I had one appearance before the committee. A member of my staff saw the amendments which we are now debating written on a document dated September 29. In other words, the Senate had already made its decision on the amendments before I appeared before their committee. It then reported to the House. The Senate was to debate the matter two weeks ago, but it was not possible because the Liberal Leader in the Senate was in Scotland and he wanted to speak. The Senators were going to discuss the matter last Tuesday, but again it was not possible because my remarks from the committee on October 3 were not yet translated. Then the Senators were to discuss the Bill on Wednesday, but the Governor General had need for the Red Chamber. Finally, on Thursday with one speaker from each side, the Senate sent the Bill back.
I challenge anyone to suggest seriously that what we have been exposed to over the last six or seven months is cold, analytical, non-partisan sober second thought. 1 challenge anyone to describe that as sober second thought.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me very quickly indicate that among the amendments sent by the Senate, there is one amendment that seeks to improve the quality of the translation between French and English, and in fact the amendment of the Senate does that and we certainly find that acceptable.
The Senate was of the impression that the rules respecting drugs which are researched, discovered and patented in Canada might be exempt from the requirement to keep prices lower than the cost of living. Our officials disagree with that observation, but certainly the amendment in that regard proposed by the Senate gives added assurance, and in that regard is acceptable.
The other amendments deal with three fundamental questions. The suggestion was made by the Senate that the provision dealing with what is called pipeline drugs and I will define them in a moment, be retroactive. The Bill acknowledges that between the old regime prior to Bill C-22 and the new regime which would be in place after Bill C-22 is passed,
November 3, 1987

some drugs are caught in between, in the pipeline for approval. That was the reason the Government signed a protocol on February 22, 1985, almost two years ago, providing that there be a halt to applications and processing of compulsory licence applications pending the introduction of the new Bill.
In the event, the protocol fell apart, and applications continued to stream in for compulsory licences, so after much negotiation and discussion, it was decided by the Government that for those drugs, there would be a special time period during which the brand name drug would have a period of exclusivity. The rules were that if a compulsory licence had been applied for and granted prior to June 27, 1986, the patentee would have seven years of exclusivity. If an application for compulsory licence had been applied for but not yet granted by June 27, 1986, the patentee would have an eight-year period of exclusivity. Anything applied for after that, of course, is 10 years of exclusivity.
Senators have suggested that the June 27, 1986, date is retroactive, so they have eliminated through amendments that provision and said that the Act will come into force when it is proclaimed. We have difficulty with that. First, it violates the agreement that we had negotiated with all parties over almost two years, a year and a half at that point in time. It would be a very bad precedent for Parliament to say that the Government cannot honour an agreement which in essence it entered into with all parties concerned after much discussion.
Then there is the question of retroactivity. Why is that offensive in itself? People make plans based on their interpretation of the law and the rules. It has been deemed unfair by the courts, and certainly by Parliament, to come along and say that the rules under which someone has been operating under for the last year and a half were not really the rules and we are now changing the law. If we were to accept the Senate amendments and do away with the June 26, 1986, date in the Act, we would be saying to all those companies who have based their behaviour until now on that date that they were wrong, that is not the correct date. That would be retroactive and detrimental. It is for that reason that we cannot accept the Senate amendments in this respect. We believe it to be inappropriate and a bad precedent to do so.
There is a second group of amendments which deal with the question of research and development commitments. The Senate has said, in debate and through its amendments, that if we have a commitment from the industry to spend 10 per cent of sales on research, why not write it into the law and make it specific?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I will explain why not. First, the commitment is an industry commitment, not company by company. There is an important difference. It may well be that there will be companies who spend 8 per cent of sales on research, or 6 per cent. There will be companies who spend 10 per cent, 12 per cent, 14 per cent. The commitment we have, and what the
Patent Act
industry will be held accountable to, is the over-all average. On an annual basis Parliament will receive the report of the drug prices review board and that will allow us to monitor whether the performance requirements have been met.
In addition, it is also bad law because it will negatively affect their behaviour. Let me give you some hypothetical examples. A new small company, perhaps Canadian but it is not its nationality but its size that is relevant, has one or two new products. It is typical in the industry that when a new product hits the market, sales start out rather slowly because physicians do not immediately jump to use a new product. They want some assurance that it is going to work properly for their patients and so on. If it turns out that the drug is valuable in the treatment of disease, then sales start to go up.
You could have a small Canadian company spending 10 per cent or 15 per cent of its sales on research while selling at a certain rate, and then if sales of the drug start to take off in the latter quarter of the year, they would have to halt sales because their sales to research ratio for that year would be knocked out of whack and they would lose their patent. It would have the effect of triggering undesirable behaviour by a company in order to meet a rigid numerical test.
Another not uncommon practice for companies with a limited number of products is to buy other companies so that their salesmen have a complete line of products. For example, most drug companies have a line of over-the-counter drugs such as cough medicines, headache remedies, stomach remedies and so on. If a new company were starting up with a limited number of patented drugs and wanted to complement its sales line by buying an over-the-counter operation, it might not be able to do that if the total sales of the group caused its R and D ratio to be knocked out of whack.
Bear in mind that research and development cannot be turned off and on like a spigot. You do not go down to the local UIC office and hire Ph.D.s in biochemistry. It takes a long time to get a research program under way. Planning is required and you are not able to respond that quickly. By having a rigid numerical formula for each and every company, you could trigger behaviour that nobody wants.
Another possibility, based on the Senate amendments, is that a company would restructure itself so that it hold its valuable patents and does its research in one company and everything else in the other. It would be very easy to meet the research targets spelled out in the Senate amendments through the one company, while the other company has no patents and therefore it does not really matter whether it has any research or not because no penalties can be imposed under the provisions of the Act.
While the intent of the Senate may be the same as ours, to achieve a spending level on research of 10 per cent of sales, while the argument for writing it into the law sounds reasonable at first blush, in fact it is not a good law and not the right way to go. For that reason I recommend that this House not accept those amendments.

November 3, 1987
Patent Act
The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte Marie (Mr. Malepart), in a radio interview, said that at end of the day we are going to be accountable if the industry fails to meet the R and D requirements. The Government that introduced the legislation is going to be accountable. However, the Government of the day will have the ability to go back to the old rules after four years. The Government of the day will have sufficient power to make sure that the industry meets those levels. If it does not do so, it will be accountable to the people in the election, and that is the way it ought to be.

Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), is going to be the Prime Minister, he should know, and he does, that the Government of the day will be able to undo this legislation by Order in Council. No Bill is necessary. If he is confident about being the Government, then he should have no difficulty in helping us get this motion through.
There is a third group of proposed amendments which would put in a rigid numerical test which says that the cost of a drug should not increase more than the cost of living as indicated by the Consumer Price Index. That is the intent of the legislation. The Senate says if that is the intent, write it in and be absolutely specific. That is bad law. I remind the House that when we had runaway inflation, the Anti-Inflation Board was there to make sure that prices and wages did not increase beyond specific levels. However, there was always flexibility to allow for exceptional cases. Good law provides flexibility.
Let me give a hypothetical example. A company has a new drug on the market and it is very useful in treating certain diseases but it has a negative side effect for 10 per cent of its users as a result of an impurity. By spending more money the company can remove that impurity or reduce the unfortunate side effects to 1 per cent, but to recover the cost it would have to increase the price more than the cost of living. The company would, in essence, be precluded from doing what might be appropriate for medicinal reasons because if it did so the Act would require that the company lose its patent automatically and without judgment. I do not think we should have law which contains such a provision.
There could be dozens of reasons why a particular drug may merit an increase of more than the increase in the cost of living in a particular year. The Senate apparently believes that the drug prices review board will not be in a position to ensure that that happens. The head of that board, Dr. Eastman, believes that the board has the power.
However, in order to give added assurance we are suggesting that Clause 15 be amended by adding, after line 36 on page
13, that if, in the opinion of the board, a patentee has increased the price in excess of the Consumer Price Index, the board can require that patentee to provide detailed financial information on how the price of a drug was set to enable the board to make a judgment. If the board makes a request under this provision, it will be required, in its subsequent annual report, to report that it made a request of that company and to give its reasons for its judgment, whether to allow the increase or to take away the patent.
We think this is an unnecessary addition, that the board would be effective without this, but we will put it in black and white in the law. One of the consequences of the activity of the Senate is to raise once again the spectre of whether drug prices will increase at a faster rate than the cost of living. They will not. 1 maintain that those who claim that they will are wrong and have no basis for making that claim.
However, it has been repeated so frequently that, as is the case with many things which are repeated again and again, a case has been established by virtue of repetition rather than by virtue of any foundation. That being the case, it is perhaps not unreasonable to give added assurance to the public that drug price increases will be less than increases in the cost of living except where clearly justified and justifiable.
That is the basis for the amendments. We cannot accept what the Senate is proposing. We believe that its proposal to make every company meet rigid numerical tests in research and development will lead to avoidance, distort business decisions, and could be unfair in some cases.
By way of rationale, it is very common for companies to sell drugs on licence. The most successful drug company today according to the stock market is Merck. Merck will be introducing a new anti-peptic ulcer drug called Pepsum but the patent will actually belong to a Japanese company. Merck will be selling it in North America on licence from the Japanese company.
Since you cannot take away from Merck a patent that they do not have, the inadvertent effect of the Senate's proposal would be to exclude from consideration this drug, which may or may not be very important in terms of revenues to Merck but which, in my view, should be considered when deciding whether Merck is doing its 10 per cent of sales on research. I think that should involve the judgment of the House and future Governments. The drug prices review board should be published, but a rigid numerical test is simply bad law. It is bad not to permit judgment in these instances.
With regard to the cost of living, we believe that under the original Bill C-22 the drug prices review board would have kept increasing the cost of all drugs, including that 80 per cent which never attracts any generic competitors, under increases in the cost of living. We must remember that when there is no generic interest in a drug taking away the patent is hardly a penalty.
November 3, 1987

We are convinced that the drug prices review board will work. We believe that the annual exposure of the public to drug prices will have a significant downward impact. However, because the concern that prices will rise has been repeated ad nauseam, although it has never been established on any rational basis and is only a propaganda technique, some people have started to believe it.
Therefore, to give added assurance we are proposing these amendments which empower the board to do that which I am sure it would have been able to do anyway, that is, to examine in detail the rationale for any price increases above the cost of living, to make a judgment as to whether or not they are appropriate, and to report annually on the fact that it has made the analysis and on why it has accepted or rejected the price increase in each instance.
I believe that that provides suspenders on top of a belt, but it should keep the pants up and be doubly assuring to those who are nervous.

CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-OPINION OF HON. MITCHELL SHARP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the issue of free trade, we heard this morning that a freer trader by the name of Mitchell Sharp thinks this is a bad deal. The reason he thinks it is a bad deal is not because he is against liberalized trade but because he feels that this particular deal will compromise Canada. We are pitting a strong partner against a weak partner in a continentalist approach to trading as opposed to opening our eyes, our arms, and our markets to the whole world.
In fact this issue is not about free trade; it is about a bad Mulroney deal which is selling out Canadian interests in energy, culture, and economics for the all-mighty American buck. A point was made today in the committee when somebody said there is a price to pay for being a Canadian. We heard a Conservative member ask in a snarky fashion, "What price?"
The continentalist pull which has had its historic impact on this country is such that if we do not develop and continue to nurture an east-west trading relationship among the provinces, we will be taking the first step toward absorption by the United States. That is what this issue is all about. It is about keeping Canada together. It is about a bad economic and cultural deal that could cost Canada our sovereignty.
We on this side of the House believe that Canadians are entitled to all the facts on the deal. We want a full and open discussion because we believe Canadians will reject this bad Mulroney deal when they finally see the fine print. The Government wants to ram it through because it knows it will not stand up to the scrutiny of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Orders, I gave you notice of my intention to rise on a matter of privilege and to introduce a motion of referral to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges

November 3, 1987
Question of Privilege-Mr. Jourdenais
and Procedure. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I could proceed immediately.
The House will surely know that the election of the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration was quite an exciting and even very noisy event on Wednesday, October 7, 1987, around 3:30 p.m. The officers to be elected were the chairman and vice-chairman of the committee. The minutes and proceedings are to be found in Issue No. 42 of the Minutes of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, page 4212, where the qualifications of the nominees, namely myself, the Hon. Member for Laprairie (Mr. Jourdenais), and the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier), were discussed.
During the sitting, a member of the Committee asked Mr. Lanthier whether he was parliamentary secretary. Another Member, Mr. John Oostrom, took his defense, stating-excuse me, the Member who sponsored Mr. Lanthier's nomination, in reply to Mr. Warren Allmand, had this to say: To my knowledge, Mr. Lanthier is no longer a parliamentary secretary. Another Member, Mr. Rodriguez, asked him: Is Mr. Lanthier parliamentary secretary at this point or not? Mr. Lanthier answered: I am not, at least I do not think I am. Mr. Rodriguez: You do not think your are, well are you or are you not? Mr. Lanthier said: I am no longer, at least I do not think so. I said goodbye yesterday to the Minister and the Deputy Minister of Public Works. Please note that this happened on October 7, 1987.
Now, at the end of last week, the Government tabled the Public Accounts of Canada. I examined them in detail on Friday, especially Volume II, and the additional information and analyses on page 1209 of the Public Accounts, 1986-87, where the salaries of parliamentary secretaries to Ministers are listed, and there I saw the entry: Lanthier, C-which means Claude-Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works-October 15, 1986, to October 16, 1987, with a $9,450 salary.
Mr. Speaker, I was taken aback because I remembered vividly the answers given by Mr. Lanthier on October 7.
Mr. Speaker, ever since I was elected to the House of Commons, I have always assumed with humility my role as a Member of this House and I have a great deal of respect for this institution. Since last Friday, I have made inquiries and even went to the Privy Council Office where Mr. Chasse confirmed that the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) had not resigned as a Parliamentary Secretary and that he still held that job on October 14. All other Parliamentary Secretaries were appointed on October 14, with their appointment effective on the 15th. Therefore, Mr. Lanthier was still a Parliamentary Secretary and he was still paid accordingly.
I had consultations with parliamentarians and experts in different Parliaments and even in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. I quote a committee chairman, who
should be, like the Speaker of the House, above all suspicion, partisanship, and conflicts of interest and who should be straightforward.
Mr. Speaker, I hasten to add that I raise this issue which is so essential for the proper functioning of the House as a good parliamentarian who seeks to uphold the respectability of this House, of its members and Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, this is probably the first time such a question of privilege is raised by a Member on the Government side about one of his colleagues in the same Party. As recently as last week, all those present in the House heard the Prime Minister confirm the importance of the McGrath reform.
On October 7, when the election was held, the presence of shock troops, of groups that have been called "goons" could be noticed. Even the assistant Whip for the Government, the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) was there to lead the Government troops with his advisers. It is impossible to plead ignorance or forgetfulness. The Hon. Member for LaSalle is a well-known professional engineer. Precision and accuracy are part of his psychology. He made a false statement and the election is therefore invalid. Members of the Committee and of the House have been misled. The Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) should resign immediately as chairman of the Committee. On Bill C-22 the Minister tried to give the impression that what was happening at the present time was unprecedented. That is not the case. When disagreements like this one occurred in the past, conferences were held between the Senate and the House of Commons, and they were held at this stage, that is, when the Senate has twice sent back a government Bill. Instead of following the normal procedure and holding a conference, as has been done in the past, the Government of Canada has acted on its own, proposing new amendments without any consultation whatsoever.

I say it is a shame that the NDP Leader, for whatever reasons, is not here in the Chamber to address those concerns as evidenced by the comments of that Member.
In order to give effect to the statements made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) that prices of drugs will not increase faster than the increase in inflation, Bill C-22 was amended to reflect the Minister's own words. I must point out that the Minister responsible has been telling Canadians from coast to coast that the Prices Review Board will keep price increases at less than the cost of living. When he appeared before the special Senate committee on Bill C-22 on April 14, 1987, the Minister said:
Under the legislation, the Drug Prices Review Board will have a mandate to examine the prices of all drugs and to keep the prices less than the rise in increase in inflation.
That is found at page 28. On August 20, 1987, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs told Members of the House the following:
The Drug Prices Review Board will be in place and mandated by law to keep those prices increases at less than the cost of living. Thus for the first time we will have those drugs for which there is no generic competitor being held down in terms of price increases by the Drug Prices Review Board.
That is found at page 8249. On the following day the same Minister repeated the same message to the House. He said:
This package. Bill C-22, provides consumer protection ... It provides that drugs will not increase more than the cost of living.
He went on to say:
Under our scheme the Drug Prices Review Board will be examining those drugs and keeping the price increases of them at less than the cost of living.
That was the Minister responsible in this House and across the country for consumers.
The amendment which was suggested by the Senate Banking, Trade and Commerce Committee provides that the Consumer Price Index should be the primary factor which the Prices Review Board considers rather than merely one of many factors. The thrust of the amendment of the Upper Chamber is that the primary consideration be the Prices Review Board and that is in accordance with the Minister's own statement. Should the price of a drug increase faster than the Consumer Price Index, the manufacturer would then lose its period of exclusivity on that drug and at the board's discretion, its period of exclusivity on any additional drug. This amendment is in total conformity with the Minister's own words. If he will not agree to this amendment or to the thrust of this amendment, perhaps he could explain to Canadians and to Members of this House why he refuses to include in the Bill guarantees that reflect his very own words. If he does not accept this amendment, which is evidenced by his comments here, let him
Patent Act
then confirm that price increases in excess of inflation will be permitted.
I suggest to the Minister, to his Cabinet colleagues and to the Members of this House that the Minister responsible for consumers cannot and should not have it both ways. He has to choose.
The second area of substantive amendments deals with research and development. At second reading debate in the House of Commons on November 20, 1986, the same Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs stated:
We have received commitments from the industry to invest directly in research and development $1.4 billion and to create 3,000 jobs between now and 1995. The commitment is worded so that 10 per cent of sales will be invested in research and development.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, those words, those commitments are found nowhere in Bill C-22. They are not in the Bill. They are not in an exchange of letters as was the case, if you will, with the Auto Pact. These commitments are contained in what? In press releases. What Canadians are asked to put their reliance in is the promise and the weight of a press release. The Government seems to talk with perverse pride in the fact that it has not obtained a firm undertaking or guarantees from the very companies which would so handsomely, and I underline the word handsomely, profit from this legislation. This approach in my view is both naive and unacceptable.
In 1985 the Government of Canada introduced a 10 per cent sales tax on non-prescription drugs such as Aspirin and cold remedies and even poison ivy treatments. Now, the implementation of a tax on medicine is in itself scandalous. Does an individual who falls ill not face enough adversity without being taxed on the very medication he or she must purchase to treat his or her ailment? Apparently not in the view of the Government. When it comes to collecting additional revenues from the ill, the sick, the Government has absolutely no hesitation in codifying such measures in the very law of Canada to ensure that it collects its own reward in the form of a sales tax. There is no hesitation, no doubt. It is a clear unequivocal desire to implement sales tax on the sick and on the elderly.
Contrast this approach to the one being taken in the legislation before us. The Government of Canada assures us that the pharmaceutical manufacturers will increase research and development expenditures by a total of SI.4 billion over the next 10 years. But there is nothing, absolutely nothing, not a comma, not a sentence, not a reference, not an amendment, absolutely nothing in the Bill that requires the Government to do so. Over a billion dollars is reportedly at stake. The Government and, indeed, right now the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) laugh. They hold up press releases and then they cry victory. It is shameful, shameful behaviour on the part of a national Government which is supposed to take its responsibility both seriously and sincerely.

November 3, 1987

The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs went on and stated before the special committee on Bill C-22, "1 prefer a carrot to a stick. I don't think a stick is necessary". He said that on April 14, 1987. No, Mr. Speaker, one would certainly not want to use a stick on the multinational pharmaceutical interests. When it comes to taxing Canadians who fall ill, this Government apparently has no hesitation in holding the stick over their heads. I ask government Members where is the fairness, where is the social justice, where is the dignity? I suggest it is highly lacking and that is evidenced by their actions.
Is the goal of the Government to promote research and development in Canada? The people in the Senate did their best to further that goal by providing amendments to Bill C-22. They recommended that a pharmaceutical royalty fund be created, the same recommendation that was made by one of Canada's most distinguished authorities, Dr. Harry Eastman. Drug companies would receive additional monies in direct proportion to the amount of research they conduct. The Government found this unacceptable. It prefers to give a blank cheque to the pharmaceutical giants to be paid by the sick, the elderly and the infirm of Canada.
The Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, in the spirit of compromise, now recommends that at the very least, the promises of the Minister and of the pharmaceutical companies be placed in the legislation itself. Surely if the Minister believes in his own words, if the industry, as evidenced by the press releases of the pharmaceutical multinationals, believes in its own words, what do they have to fear? If what they have said will be realized, why would they be afraid? What do they have to hide?
The Senate did not ask for any additional commitments. It is not substituting a totally new scheme in place of that proposed by the Government. The Senate amendments simply ask that the promises made by the industry be contained in the legislation and nothing more.
The amendments would require the drug companies to actually spend the funds they have promised to spend on research and development. If the drug companies are serious about the commitments they have made in Quebec, Ontario and other parts of Canada, they should have no reason for concern because this amendment would never, ever come into effect. It would only come into effect if those companies and the industries at large reneged on their promises and failed to live up to their commitments.
This amendment is obviously unacceptable to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I would ask the Minister to take the time to explain to the employees of the pharmaceutical industry why he refuses to put into the Bill a guarantee that research and development will actually increase as promised by the industry and now by the Minister.
As introduced by the Government, Bill C-22 does not even require pharmaceutical companies to maintain their present levels of research and development and employment, let alone increase them. That is shameful national social policy. What kind of Government would be that irresponsible to the people it says it represents and wishes to represent?
If the Government says that research and development will increase to 10 per cent of sales, and if the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada is making the same commitment, why is there hesitation about putting it in the Bill? Let me use this analogy. If a consumer went to buy a car, a fridge, a stove or any other commodity and the salesman made all sorts of promises about the vehicle, the fridge or the stove, but then at the end of the day when the consumer went to pay for that particular commodity, the salesman refused to put any of those promises in writing, would the consumer not have some serious concerns and reservations about the promises? I think the answer is obvious to most Canadians.
If the Government refuses to put into writing its own words, then all Canadians have good reason for concern. It is not fair, it is not good public policy, it is not in the interests of Canadians, it is not in the interests of trying to maintain reasonable prices for prescription drugs for the Government to give away without receiving anything in return.
I underline again and again the unfairness, the incompetence, the give-away, the walk-away about the objectives of social policy. Why is the Government afraid to put into legislation things it has been telling Canadians from coast to coast? Unfortunately, the reasons for the Government's refusal are what we in the Opposition have been echoing for quite some time.
The Minister may say, as he attempted to say in committee, that for certain technical reasons, this amendment cannot be accepted, but it can be accepted. It only requires the political will to do so. There could have been that will, as evidenced by the suggestions we made in committee and in the House and our colleagues made in the Senate. If there was one iota, one teensy little bit of political will on the other side to protect Canadians from the harshness of this particular Bill and to give us guarantees for research and development, jobs and the protection of the consumer, the Government would have moved on those suggestions.
Canadians now hold the position, as evidenced by opposition across the country, that this Government does not really believe what it has told us. It is a smoke and mirrors game. Say one thing, do the complete opposite. The Government did it on free trade. In 1983, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said no way to free trade. Now free trade is here. The same thing was true with the sacred trust. He put legislation in to deindex pensions for senior citizens. The list goes on and on.
Who have been hit? Who pays for these unconscionable acts of the Government? It is the Canadian consumer who pays.
November 3, 1987

The third area of amendment deals with the retrospective operation of Bill C-22. We heard today a litany of words and sentences piled up on top of one another by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. One would have to be a Philadelphia lawyer, a medical surgeon and a Ph.D. in biochemistry to understand what he was talking about. He did not know what he was talking about.
As a matter of principle, legislation with a retrospective application is highly objectionable. Bill C-22 is no exception. The committee found that the use of June 27, 1986, as the operative date impairs the rights of certain licensees and of those who have applied for but have not yet been granted compulsory licences. The Minister tries to weave, bob, stand on this foot and stand on that foot to justify using the date of June 27, 1986.
Some have said the Minister is on drugs. I do not believe that for one moment. I think he has taken the drug and right now he is coming off it. That is why he is making such silly, stupid and irresponsible statements as he made here this morning. I wish we had the opportunity to have him in the Chamber in order to have a frank and free-flowing debate on some of those irresponsible and somewhat incompetent statements regarding the retroactivity of Bill C-22.
Generic companies have expended time and money under the present legislation. They have applied for compulsory licences and notices of compliance in good faith. We are now told by the Government that those efforts are to be of no avail because the law is to be changed as of June, 1986. Where is the fairness? The Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kem-pling), who sat on the committee studying this Bill, referred with great eloquence to the generic companies as nothing more than rapists. That was his understanding of the contribution generic companies can make to the pharmaceutical industry. Members opposite have a very narrow view of the industry. It is based on one foundation, that of the multinational corporation. We in this Party believe it is more than just that group. It is the generic industry, the Canadian consumer, provincial Governments, and other interested groups across this country.
The unfairness of the retroactivity involved in this legislation is without parallel. What is particularly disturbing is that the companies which will be harmed are in the main Canadian generic companies. Not only do we bring in harmful retroactive legislation, it is most harmful to the Canadian generic industry. So much for helping Canadian business. So much for trying to facilitate expansion of the Canadian pharmaceutical industry. The Government is doing everything but.
I want to underline that the obvious beneficiaries of Bill C-22 are foreign based multinational companies. Let us be clear. It is one thing to say, as the Minister said, that new jobs will be created, research and development will take place, and prices will be maintained in line with the CPI. It is quite another thing for him to say, because of a magical process called the press release, that we should place our faith in multinational corporations with respect to creating jobs, increasing research and development, and maintaining
Patent Act
reasonable prices. The Minister is out to lunch, he does not know what he is talking about, when he relies solely on the press releases of multinational corporations.
There is of course an argument to be made that all firms operating in Canada should be treated equally. In this instance the Government seems to have gone out of its way to hinder development of a Canadian controlled pharmaceutical industry. What the Senate Banking, Trade and Commerce Committee has done is to recommend that the Bill be amended to provide that the new regime would only come into effect on the date the Bill is proclaimed. It says that this new regime would apply only to brand name drugs that received their notice of compliance on or after that date. In this way new drugs would be afforded the increased protection of Bill C-22, while drugs now on the market would continue to be governed by the old rules.
What is so earth shattering about that suggestion? Why could the Minister not accept the thrust of that amendment? Has he made a side deal with the multinational corporations which he refuses to inform Parliament about? That is the conclusion Canadians are coming to. The Minister refuses to codify his own words in this legislation. Surely any fair, reasonable and objective individual would have to conclude that there must have been some side deal in order that we revert not to June of 1987 but June of 1986.
That is a long period of time. 1 am sure even you, Mr. Speaker, reasonable and objective man that you are, coming from that great Province of Alberta which is opposed to higher drug prices, can see the insensitivity on the part of the Minister regarding the Senate's amendment concerning retroactivity. Who is it going to hurt or hinder? Canadian consumers? The generic industry? The employees of those generic firms, a point which has not been mentioned in this House as of yet?
There are other objections to this Bill. The amendments proposed by the Senate Banking, Trade and Commerce Committee are reasonable and deserving of our support. There is nothing in these amendments, absolutely nothing, to cause any discomfort to the Government, particularly since they mirror the Government's own words. I would like to draw to the attention of Members of this House comments made in a Financial Post editorial on October 26, 1987. If anything, that paper has not been overly fair, understanding or sensitive to the views of opposition Members about this Bill, nor to the Senate's view, nor indeed the whole issue of intellectual property rights. However, for the edification of Members opposite I want to quote what The Financial Post had to say. It says in part:
The Government seems determined to manufacture a constitutional impasse over its drug patents law, Bill C-22. It was one thing for the Senate to alter fundamentally the nature of the bill, as it did in its first round of amendments. It is quite another when, the bill having been returned to the upper house, a Senate committee suggests the most moderate, sympathetic amendments, wholly in keeping with the spirit of the legislation and respecting every constitutional precedent-only to meet with brusque dismissal from Consumer & Corporate Affairs Minister Harvie Andre.

November 3, 1987

The Senate banking, trade & commerce committee's recommendations only sharpened the bill's purpose, that it might at least achieve what it intends. One sets explicit guidelines for the new drug price review board. A second established R&D commitments in law, on a company-by-company basis, rather than industry-wide. And a third merely cancels the bill's retroactivity, in accord with natural justice. In every essential, including the 10-year monopoly for new drugs, the bill is intact. Consumers, taxpayers, and economists might have complaints at this, but the minister should have none.
Finally, it says:
-the government should surely be able to accept the Senate amendments and spare us a constitutional showdown.
Mr. Speaker, that was in the The Financial Post of October 26, 1987, in an article entitled "Drugs and trade", commenting on the amendments which have been referred to us in this Chamber for our	consideration-reasonable, objective
amendments being put forward, not to lessen the government thrust of Bill C-22 but to improve it and to codify and confirm the words of the Minister responsible.
The Minister has come into this Chamber and insulted my colleagues from the Province of Quebec. He has made reference to opposition Members using stalling tactics. On a previous occasion this Minister accepted amendments of the Senate and then went on to make two additional amendments himself.
I do not know whether the Minister was speedreading, talking in his sleep, talking as he was coming off drugs, or what, but he seemed to suggest in his motion that he was accepting one of our amendments and some other amendments, the full impact of which we are in the process of examining. The Minister has certainly not gone far enough in my view.
In this debate we must emphasize the position which our Party has taken from day one. It was the NDP which said "no amendments to Bill C-22, none whatsoever". That was a couple of months ago. There was then some wavering and then they wanted some amendments, in fact they even suggested some amendments. When the standing committee met, some amendments were brought to Parliament but they were rejected by the Government. Today the senior member of the New Democratic Party from British Columbia says that we should do away with the Senate, that it should have no right to improve Bill C-22.
I am not suggesting that that is hypocrisy. I am not suggesting that they are sitting on the fence wavering back and forth, waiting for a political opportunity to jump in or jump out. I would not say that about the members of the New Democratic Party. They do not know where they are at. If the convention is in Montreal, they are against Bill C-22. If the convention is in Atlantic Canada, they are probably against Bill C-22.
It is clear to Members in this Party that the New Democratic Party has been, as I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will agree, inconsistent throughout this entire debate. That ought to be brought to the attention of the House.
I know that my colleagues across the way are very much aware of their inconsistency, of the way they change their feet, pulling one foot out and putting the other foot in to meet the political whims of the day, whatever they may be. First they wanted no amendments, then they wanted amendments, and now they want no more amendments. Are they in support of Bill C-22 or are they against it? I think Canadians should know where they stand. We have seen in this House a terrible display of inconsistency by members of that Party. They do not know where they are at and I suppose they never will.
We, however, have been consistent throughout. We have said since day one that there must be amendments to the Patent Act. The Government has advocated a 10-year monopoly period for the multinational corporations. The Minister of Justice has a social conscience and I know that he agrees with me-although he cannot say anything because of cabinet solidarity-that that was the wrong way for the Government to proceed. I know that my good friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, also agrees that it was a Draconian measure taken against the consumers of the country to include a 10-year period of exclusivity. The Minister of Justice shakes his head. I do not know whether he is blowing his nose or what.

As a physician, I am aware of the difficulties some patients are having paying for drugs. It is important that we take whatever steps are necessary to keep drug prices lower .. . I also have a letter that was sent to the Minister, to whom I have referred in a very kind way. I refer to him as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but from time to time I do make mistakes. My mistake is that I have been generous and kind. I have called him the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but I tell you that he is the Minister of corporate affairs.

As a Chairman of a Department of Psychiatry which deals with hundreds of individuals who require certain medications to get through life, 1 am constantly reminded of the need to keep drug costs at an absolute minimum. Many other Canadians are opposed to Bill C-22. I do not wish to reiterate all of those groups and organizations who have opposed it, but it must be said for the benefit of Members and indeed the Canadian public that six provincial Governments are opposed to Bill C-22. Yet we only hear from the Government benches that one government, the Government of Quebec, supports Bill C-22.
I have stated in this Chamber on several occasions that we support research and development, we support jobs, we support the lessening of price increases and the maintenance of reasonable prices for prescription drugs. That is why we have attempted both in the House of Commons and in the Senate to effect amendments which would serve that purpose. Yet the Government has chosen not to do that, for whatever reasons.
Let it be said clearly and unequivocally that the amendments which have been put forward by our Party and our colleagues in the Senate have been made to strengthen the Bill and provide Quebecers with those assurances on jobs, research and development and a guarantee with regard to the cost of prescription drugs. The Minister began by telling us that there will be all sorts of benefits for all Canadians, those who live in western Canada, Atlantic Canada, Ontario and Quebec. The Minister then said that perhaps he should change that to mean the capitals of the various provinces would benefit. Now he has sliced off the Atlantic, thrown out western Canada. Perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare would accept the challenge to take the truthfulness of the comments of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs as well as the truthfulness of the multinational corporations, and take that truthfulness-if he believes so strongly in their truthfulness-and place it into law so that all Canadians can see and recognize that their words really mean something, that they do not have to depend upon the mere words and weight of a press release that may have been issued from the head office of the multinational corporation or, indeed, from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I think the Minister might want to do that for Canadians if he is so concerned about truthfulness.
We have heard the Minister talk about the great benefits that would be bestowed upon Canada with Bill C-22. The area now being concentrated on is the City of Montreal. We are told all sorts of benefits will go to Montreal. I am not against benefits going to Montreal. My colleagues are not against benefits going to Montreal. I just ask the Hon.
