PROPOSED ERECTION OF STATUE OF QUEEN ELIZABETH II The House resumed from Friday, October 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Tupper:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of commissioning the structure of a statue of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, to be placed on Parliament Hill in commemoration of the thirty-fifth anniversary of Her ascension to the Throne.

Mr. Speaker, I count it an honour indeed to have the opportunity to speak on the motion introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean- Carleton (Mr. Tupper) and seconded by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil). The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of commissioning the structure of a statue of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, to be placed on Parliament Hill, in commemoration of the thirty-fifth anniversary of Her ascension to the Throne.
I strongly support this motion, Mr. Speaker. Over the years in my public life I have had the opportunity of watching, seeing and speaking to Her Majesty the Queen. The first instance I had of meeting the Queen was before her ascension to the Throne when she was still a princess. She toured Canada and came to Edmonton. A reception was held in the Banff Springs Hotel and 1 remember the next day the Premier telling us that the Princess had a real sense of humour. He had his speech written on cards. While having dinner he was looking over these cards and the Princess said to him "What would happen if I took those cards and shuffled them? What kind of a speech would come out then?" The Premier remarked that it would have been a very odd speech if she had shuffled the cards. I was very impressed with her way of meeting people as though they were members of her family. She has a tremendous love for people.
I have met the Queen on other occasions. Every time I have had the opportunity of meeting her, seeing her or listening to her my affection and my loyalty has increased.
When I was in opposition 1 had the opportunity of spending a week or two in London with the Parliamentary Association. During the week Commonwealth Day occurred. There were 23 of us from various Commonwealth countries at the meeting. We were invited by Her Majesty the Queen to have tea with her and the Duke. People were there from China, Hong Kong and the various islands. We were a group of Commonwealth
Statue of Monarch
members of all colours, creeds and political Parties. I will never forget the tea we had with Her Majesty. She took the opportunity to speak to every one of the delegates. She asked people about their countries and how conditions were. When she spoke to the Liberal Member and myself, she told us she was interested in the Canadian youth. She seemed to be dedicated to doing something for youth, which made me very pleased.
A few days later we celebrated Commonwealth Day. We ceased our studies that day and went to Westminster Abbey where a beautiful service was held. It was a lovely tribute to Her Majesty. Representatives of every Commonwealth country were there with their flags. As the various people came in following Her Majesty into the Abbey she said how proud she was to be the Queen of such a tremendous group of people.
I kept a copy of the speech Her Majesty gave that day.
I would like to refer to a few things she said about the people of the Commonwealth. Speaking about Commonwealth Day, she said:
First and foremost, it is about people, and particularly about the young. In many countries they make up nearly half the population. At its most spectacular and exhilarating it is about athletes such as I saw last year competing brilliantly in the unique atmosphere of the Commonwealth Games; at its most enchanting it is about the children who gave me such a welcome on my first visits to some of the island nations in the Pacific Ocean; but fundamentally it is concerned with all those who in their early years have to learn how best to meet the challenges of living in the world today.
As I heard Her Majesty say that, I thought here is the head of a wonderful group of nations who is down to earth and knows how to express the feelings of the people over whom she reigns. She did not tell them what was good for them. She was trying to assist them in meeting their challenges. The Queen went on to say:
This is why, through its youth program, its technical and professional programs, and its work in the field of health and education, the Commonwealth helps to tackle the problems of underemployment and undernourishment and to provide opportunities for millions of families to achieve the fulfilment in life which is their natural right.
As the Queen talked about undernourishment, I thought what a challenge it is that she is giving us to help those who do not get enough or the wrong kind of food and to help those who are not educated. I thought how often in Canada people reluctantly go to school wondering why they have to spend so much time there. Yet almost half of the boys and girls of the world today would give their right arms or anything they have of value just to know how to read.
It made me think of when I was a young Grade 12 student in the Drumheller Valley. A coal miner asked me to teach him how to read. He must have been a man of 50 or 60 years old. I said "Yes. Sure, I will be glad to". It was my first attempt at pedagogy. I had a little old primer which had "This is a flower. This flower is red. This flower is blue". I went over this book with him day after day. One day he was reading to me and said "This is a flower. This flower is black". It struck me funny when he spoke about a black flower. I guess there are

November 3, 1987
Statue of Monarch
black flowers but I did not think there were in those days. 1 did not withhold my laugh. I looked at him and saw how I had hurt him. I told my mother about it when 1 got home and she asked me if I had apologized. She said that I should never say anything like that because he was learning how to read. I apologized all right. It was the first lesson I had which I have practised many times since, when teaching school. One should never do anything to hurt a youngster and stop him or her from developing in his or her own way. The coal miner eventually learned how to read and could read pretty well. I was very proud of that.
Here we had the Queen telling her subjects to help those who could not read and those who are undernourished. 1 admired that. The Queen concluded her address with:
The Commonwealth cannot of itself solve all the problems of the human race but as a world-wide community it works for peace and for the elimination of poverty.
Through the ready sharing of ideas, experience, skills and resources between governments and between people in all walks of life it seeks year by year to enrich the world in which its young people are growing up.
That was the Queen of Canada speaking. Yes, I think we should have a statue of Her Majesty the Queen. She has been a wonderful sovereign. She has set an example in living, in helping others, in sharing. I think we could do no better than to have a statue of Her Majesty the Queen on Parliament Hill here in Ottawa.
I see my time is up. There are many, many other things I would like to mention about Her Majesty but I have to stop now. I want to say that I count it an honour to be a subject of Her Majesty the Queen and I look forward to seeing, I hope before too long, a statue on this Hill put up to remember this wonderful woman for many, many years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech made by my hon. colleague. I listened very intently and it occurred to me that it is more than appropriate that we take some time to consider the role of the Queen in respect to our nation and the Commonwealth to which this nation belongs.
A very interesting comparison can be made between this country and the United States. In contrast to Canada, they have in the United States in the same person the head of state and the head of Government. We know what great difficulties and confusion are caused by that state of affairs. That can be exemplified by the Watergate era. The then President of the United States, Richard Nixon, being both head of state and head of Government, caused a great deal of concern throughout the nation as to how to deal with the question of his actions as head of Government while at the same time he was symbolic of the American nation as a whole.
If we give a little thought to it, I am sure we would realize that there are a great many Canadians who would be very upset if our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) were at the same
time head of state and head of Government. It is convenient to have a clear separation.
Of course, in addition to being the head of our state represented by the Governor General, the Queen is also the symbolic head of the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth of Nations met in Vancouver not very long ago. At that time, I was pleased to have the occasion to meet the Queen under conditions in which we were able to exchange a few words as one person to another. I must say that I was quite impressed by her basic humanity and with the way she was able to converse with common people. In the final analysis, she has blood as red as ours flowing in her veins, and on that basis, with the exception of the symbol she constitutes, she is no different from the rest of us.
1 think it is important to talk about the Queen's position with respect to the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth is a group which shares the legacy of the British Empire and has eschewed the chains of imperialism to constitute a collectivity of nations which are bound together by their common heritage across racial, religious and ethnic lines. It is a voluntary grouping of nations.
If there is any other characteristic that ought to exist in the Commonwealth of Nations, it is that there should be an absence of any element of racism. Its mission should be to ensure that in this world, and certainly among the Commonwealth nations, there be no truck with racism.
Being aware of the Queen's position on the Commonwealth's treatment of the issue of apartheid, I was very pleased to learn that she is very concerned about the refusal of the British Government led by Margaret Thatcher to join with the rest of the Commonwealth in dealing with the issue of apartheid by making it possible for this noble collection of nations to exert its power and influence upon that dreadful regime to ensure that racism be eliminated there as it must be eliminated throughout the world. We are left in a rather curious situation. The Queen, the symbol of our nation and of the Commonwealth, resides in a country whose Prime Minister refuses to act in accordance with the traditions and concerns shared by so many of this great group of nations.
Rather than constructing a stone statue of the Queen, I think the greatest monument would be a Commonwealth which has been successful in establishing unity on this very serious problem which concerns so many. If the Commonwealth can act as Canada would lead it to act, then of course the greatest monument to the Queen would be a Commonwealth that is characterized by having taken for the first time effective actions to ensure that this legacy of racism colonialism has been left behind and will be eliminated once and for all. That is the kind of monument to build to the Queen.

Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased, as are others, to have the opportunity to speak in this debate. I want to compliment my colleague from Nepean- Carleton who brought this private Member's motion to the floor for debate. I would like to put it on the record again:
November 3, 1987

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of commissioning the structure of a statue of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, to be placed on Parliament Hill in commemoration of the thirty-fifth anniversary of Her ascension to the Throne.
I was not known in my earlier years as a strong monarchist.
I had neutral feelings on it, but I have to admit that the older I get and the more experience I have in this place, the more attached I am to the monarchy, recognizing its advantages and the good it does for us as a country, for the Commonwealth and for the world in general.
I must also say that in preparing for this short presentation this afternoon, I read through the record of Hansard for the last time this motion was debated on October 2, beginning on page 9623. I note something in the speech made by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) when he introduced his motion. He answered a question that immediately came to my mind when I was first approached about speaking on this Bill this afternoon and that was, is it indeed appropriate to honour a living monarch. My assumption was that because we did not honour a living Prime Minister in such a way, we similarly would not honour a living monarch. The Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton has put that problem to rest by explaining how protocol has been set forth by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) in a recent statement. There is no problem as far as that goes at all.
I kept on reading Hansard and I came to the second speech made on that occasion by my own Member of Parliament here in Ottawa, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). I was very disappointed by his speech, I have to say. If I could summarize his speech in a few words, I would have to say that he raised all the points he possibly could as to why it would not be appropriate to have a statue of Her Majesty at this time on Parliament Hill. He asked a number of rhetorical questions but did not answer them in discussing whether or not this was a good time to do this. He said, and I quote from page 9626:
But should we do this now? If we should do it now, on what basis should we make the decision?
The Hon. Member never did answer the question. He never did say whether or not he thought it was a good idea, he just raised all these questions that would put doubt in someone's mind. I was disappointed that he as the first speaker for the NDP would take such a nihilistic attitude toward having this statue on the Hill.
The third presentation the last time this motion was up for debate was made by the Hon. Member for Renfrew- Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins). Again 1 thought he at least would be more favourably disposed to the monarchy. However, when I go through his speech he never does say he is in favour of it. He says nice things about Her Majesty, but as he got on to the topic of the statue he, as did the NDP Member, raised the spectre of the partisan debate here about the statue for former Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson. To start talking about Prime Ministers is a partisan issue. Both
Statue of Monarch
the opposition Members chose that as a reason to be less than positive about the statue for Her Majesty. The very important point raised by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) and many others is that the Queen is nonpartisan. Yet for some reason we had to get into this partisan discussion and use it as an argument against a monument to the Queen.
I have to say that I am disappointed with the lead speakers from the other two Parties who were less than enthusiastic about the idea of having a monument to the Queen.
Other speakers, including my hon. friend from Bow River, gave excellent speeches. That Hon. Member was able to interject a lot of emotion into his presentation. He also made some personal comments which I want to have the privilege of doing as well.
I happen to be a little bit proud of the fact that the Queen is less than two months older than I am. She and I are contemporaries. I followed her career with some interest partly because of that.
There is a second reason. As a young boy I began collecting postage stamps. The first Canadian stamp she appeared on was issued in 1935 to honour the Silver Jubilee of King George the Fifth, her grandfather. If memory is correct, she appears on the one-cent green stamp. The interesting thing about that stamp is the fact that on one stamp out of a plate of 100 stamps, there is a tear in her eye. That particular stamp is known as the "weeping princess" stamp. That is just a little anecdote about her first appearance on a stamp of Canadian design and it is certainly of interest to those who collect stamps.
I have a couple of other personal attachments for Her Majesty which make me very much disposed to support this motion. When she was here a few years ago my first wife and I were able to meet her in the halls of the Centre Block. There was a great gang of people there but when she saw my wife, who was in a wheelchair, she quickly moved from one side of the corridor to the other side to shake her hand. She was that kind of person. As the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said, she has a warmth and feeling for people and she has shown it on many occasions.
Finally, I had the honour some years back to exchange honours with her husband, the Duke of Edinburgh, when I was a practising physician. He and I exchanged honours at a general practitioners' meeting in the United Kingdom. Again, that makes my attachment to her and the Royal Family that much closer.
When I have occasion to speak to children in high schools I like to raise five words with them. The first three are "representative parliamentary democracy" and I go on to explain those words. They have a very intense meaning for me as a

November 3, 1987
Statue of Monarch
Member of Parliament. The other two words are "constitutional monarchy". I take great pride in explaining to those children the importance of the word "monarchy". It was alluded to by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville. Our monarch is the head of state, quite contrary to a republic or presidential system. I take great pride in explaining the advantages of a monarch who is not a partisan politician. Unfortunately, the Americans have a system where only approximately half the people have respect for the head of state. In a monarchy, 100 per cent of the people can have respect for the head of state because she is non-partisan. It is very much to her credit the way she has fulfilled that role during the last 35 years.
There are a lot of good things which have been said about the Queen and a lot of reasons why she should be honoured at this time. It is the thirty-fifth anniversary of her ascension to the throne. I was also interested to learn that she is now the longest reigning monarch we have had since Confederation. More important, since she became officially the Queen of Canada, she is the only Queen we have had as a country. That is another good reason to honour her in this way. She was the first Queen of Canada.
I see my time is coming to an end. We have a lot of buildings and hotels and other institutions which are honoured by having the Queen's name attached to them. It seems to me not unreasonable that we should consider that here on Parliament Hill. Surely there should be something on Parliament Hill to identify her in that way. I was interested to read an excerpt from the issue of Monarchy Canada of the spring of 1982. It said:
A country, to have any kind of national feeling, must have a national
memory.
Is there any better way of having that national memory of our present monarch than to erect an appropriate statue to her on Parliament Hill?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise and participate in this debate. It is very commendable that the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) saw fit to put this motion forward. I would like to take a few minutes to outline what I consider to be a very difficult job which has been handled very ably by a very classy lady.
The Queen is the head of state of a great collection of widely diverse countries with widely diverse systems of Government. As was so ably pointed out by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), she handles the problem that the Commonwealth has with South Africa with a lot of class. There is a great variety of other Governments that she has to handle just as tactfully. The Commonwealth contains a large number of countries that do not practise the same kind of democracy that we do, and she handles herself well in that respect. If you examine the make-up of the Commonwealth I am sure you will agree with that.
The most important thing for us as Canadians, the reason we should be supporting this motion, concerns her relationship with us as our head of state. She also happens to be the Queen of England, Australia and New Zealand. By act of our own
Parliament in 1953, by our own deliberate decision, she is officially and explicitly Queen of Canada, the first of many monarchs who have reigned over our territory to bear that title.

The monarchy itself is also ours by free and deliberate choice. When the Fathers of Confederation set about framing our Constitution they chose to make the new nation a constitutional monarchy. Indeed, they wanted to call it the Kingdom of Canada. The British Government was afraid that would upset the Americans and so asked the Fathers of Confederation for an alternative title. They replied with the old anglofrench word "dominion" which seemed to fit their creation like a glove. "He shall have dominion from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth".
The Fathers of Confederation did not choose constitutional monarchy only because they were used to it or because they were too stupid, too ignorant, or too much afraid of the British. They chose it in ample knowledge of the republican system which covered almost every country of the Americas. They did it deliberately and with their eyes focused not only on Canada and its position in the Commonwealth, but also taking into account the problems which it might raise with our neighbours.
I would like to relate to you, Mr. Speaker, what I see as the benefits which our nation derives from our relationship with the Queen and the Commonwealth. Our school system teaches our system of government and our relationship with the Queen. Most, if not all, Canadians treasure that system.
My relationship with the monarchy extends back to when 1 was a child and the Queen's mother and father first visited Canada. I will never forget the thrill of that first view of the Queen's mother and father. That was followed by several visits of the Queen to Canada. With each visit the thrill is not diminished but increased.
I certainly agree with the Member for Nepean-Carleton that rather than waiting until the Queen has passed on it would be a tremendous tribute to her while she is still alive for this House to authorize the erection of a statue in her honour. 1 fully support the motion of the Member for Nepean- Carleton.
[DOT]	(1740)

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to rise today to speak on the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper). Naturally, as a French-Canadian from Quebec, I do not personnally identify with royalty as closely as my Englishspeaking colleagues. For us, the Queen of England was never considered the perfect incarnation of the French fact in Canada. She is certainly a gracious Queen and we would never question her grace and the important role the British Crown has played from one generation to the next. England was a great country, and historically, it certainly gave us one of the major cultures in the world today.
November 3, 1987

Simply put, the fact is that, in my own region, we are not as thrilled by the Queen of England as people in other regions. We are not quite on the same wavelength. Naturally, a few years ago, she suddenly became the Queen of Canada. This brought her a bit closer to us. We could feel a bit more than before that she belonged to us. However, 1 believe that to motivate our young people and incite them to develop this country, we should find personalities closer to us. Such personalities might not be able to claim that their ancestors go back to the Magna Carta as does the gracious Queen Elizabeth, but they should know about the realities of this country and have lived in this British colony which we had to make our own and develop in an admittedly very hostile continent.
Once more, we are not questioning the virtues of the Queen. She has personified the respect of individual rights for an entire nation. She has personified family values, the permanence of certain values of social solidarity, but I believe that she is already ever present in Canada. She is on our dollars. She is on our stamps. She is often here in person. Her children come to see us. So do her cousins, nephews and nieces, and I believe that we always welcome them very graciously, as we would welcome our own family members. We are always very happy that they are here, but if we want to have our own personality to delevop and to define what makes our country so special and so different from England, we have to be able to identify with values which are typically our own.
Moreover, I believe that, by erecting immediately a stone statue to a Queen who is very much alive, we would be freezing her in a state from which she could no longer move. Finally, I prefer to see her here once in a while as during her last trip when she went to Saskatchewan and to Riviere-du Loup, met with the public, kissed children and spoke with adults. This seems to me much more charming and human than a stone statue on Parliament Hill.
I prefer to see the Queen as a symbol of this Commonwealth, a group of nations helping each other to develop their most democratic and humane qualities, even though some of these nations might unfortunately lag behind the others. Canada plays a very positive role in that organization. I believe that the Queen is an important symbol of the Commonwealth but, because I represent Quebec in Ottawa, I would prefer to have in this House symbols that are more representative of the French culture, which is one of the two main cultures in a multicultural Canada. I would rather have monuments that represent all of that, and consider the Queen as the symbol and the head of the Commonwealth.
I do not think that a statue of Her Majesty would mean very much for those I know in our young generation, for people in their 20's and 30's. I would rather see Her Majesty enjoy a long and happy life and keep her international role as head of the Commonwealth. Quite honestly, I do not think that a statue made of stone can play a very positive role.
Statue of Monarch
Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with this motion. I hope that we will find in our midst, within our borders, symbols that will help us promote respect for the individual and for our democratic rights. We do not need one more statue of Her Majesty. We prefer to know her as a living monarch and not as a stone statue on Parliament Hill.

Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) who, I am sure, is eloquent enough to rise and deliver them himself in this House, given his parliamentary experience. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we do not have to endorse his political views or his vision of Canada, but we must respect his philosophy, the way he upheld democracy in Canada and Quebec and particularly his strong will and integrity when leading his political party.
1 felt it was my duty, Mr. Speaker, under that motion to refer to the exceptional work of a great Quebecer and Canadian, Mr. Rene Levesque. I join all others who have already extended their deepest sympathies to the aggrieved family.
Excuse me, Mr. Speaker, if I digressed somewhat, but to come back to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper), it is a fact that we eagerly hope that the many personalities, the great men and women in Canadian history may some day be commemorated by a statue.
The Hon. Member mentioned that great efforts had been made in Canada to give public places the name of our distinguished Monarch. A special example comes to my mind, the Queen Elizabeth Hotel in Montreal. The Queen Elizabeth Hotel in Montreal was built at about the same time as our Queen came to the Throne of England, the Commonwealth Throne, and it was quite logical in my view to put up what was at that time the biggest hotel in the Montreal area. The Queen Elizabeth Hotel still has a reputation of being one of Montreal's great hotels. That is true. I am sure that this reputation of a great hotel in recognition of Our Majesty will never be tarnished in the years ahead.
Mr. Speaker, Montreal's great hotel always will keep that pride, that priviledge of bearing the name of Her Majesty the Queen of the Commonwealth.
Mr. Speaker, I think much remains to be said on the basic question, namely wether we should erect a statue to Her Majesty the Queen of Canada? Should we not at the same time, if we erect that statue while Her Majesty is quite alive, as a first step ask her permission to erect a statue of herself? I think that is absolutely essential and I do not know the answer, Mr. Speaker. And 1 think there should still be much discussion before a final decision is reached on that matter.
Mr. Speaker, I would think it quite premature to make a decision along that line, and I would invite all Members in this House-you are signalling, Mr. Speaker, that my time has already expired and I apologize for that. But 1 would invite Hon. Members in this House, before reaching a final decision on the matter, to seriously consider that possibility, that motion.
In my view, it is quite premature to come to a final decision, but I leave the floor to other Members.

Mr. Speaker, I am almost in full agreement with what the Hon. Member who has just spoken has said concerning the advisability of commissioning the erection of a statue to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of England and the Commonwealth.
First of all, it is clear that reigning for 35 years over a kingdom is something very significant and admirable; yet, because she has not yet passed away, I feel it is somewhat premature to think of placing a stone figure of her on Parliament Hill in front of the Parliament Buildings.
Needless to say, I feel that Her Majesty is far more the Queen of England and the Commonwealth, but has very little kinship with Canada, and not because of her person, for her generosity, dignity, grace, perfect command of both our official languages, and unconditional dedication to the advancement of the Commonwealth are universally recognized, not to mention her tremendous support for many humanitarian endeavours which she has often endorsed. It was pointed out, during her recent visit to Quebec, to what extent in her remarks she dealt with humanitarian issues, referring for instance to people confined to hospital beds. She has never refused to get involved when the time came to help the sick, or to do her utmost to help many Commonwealth countries progress as rapidly as other countries of the world. It goes without saying that she is universally admired and praised as a person. And I suggest that all Commonwealth countries pay tribute to her in an exemplary fashion whenever she pays them a visit.
We did so ourselves, as my honourable friend mentioned a while ago, when we welcomed her in Quebec and in Canada. People were delighted to come and greet her, and to see her, but because of her person and in part because of the tradition she is associated with.
Let us call a spade a spade: Hers is only an honorary position, without any decision making responsibility attached to it. It is not a position which contributes in any way to the advancement of our society. One even wonders whether occasionally, the reference to the Queen during Royal Assent has not been a disruptive instead of a unifying factor. When I was over in England, I happened to read an editorial in the paper, and this was about 15 years ago. The author said that since the Queen was more a factor of dissent than unity in Canada and we remember the burning issues that were creating problems at the time within Confederation well, our British editorial writer said, why not get rid of the symbol?
November 3, 1987

I think that was going a bit too far. We must keep the symbol because it means so much to one of the two founding peoples of this country. It represents a great deal, and I think that after the death of the monarch, a monument would have to be considered, since it would symbolize the links with Great Britain that presided over the birth of this nation and of all the countries of the Commonwealth.
However, a statue of the Queen is also a symbol of colonialism. We must decide whether this country's links with the Queen and with Great Britain and the monarchy have been so important we should erect a statue. Did these links make Canada the great country that it is today? Or do we owe that greatness to the two cultures and origins of two of the founding peoples of this country?
Before erecting a statue that could be seen as a symbol of colonialism, I would rather consider people like Diefenbaker, Stanfield, Trudeau or the present Prime Minister. It is to them, not to a symbol of colonialism, that Canada owes its greatness.
I think we should bear all this in mind when considering the appropriateness of erecting such a monument. I suggest we wait until Her Majesty is no longer with us, and that we consider erecting a statue as a symbol of the Commonwealth. For the time being I don't think this is particularly urgent, however, and I would invite Hon. Members to consider whether it would be appropriate to put this statue or monument in front in Parliament.
That is what 1 had to say, Mr. Speaker. My time has expired, and I hope my colleagues will agree with the point I tried to make.

FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS-PRINCIPAL SAVINGS AND TRUST-REIMBURSEMENT OF INVESTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early in August I rose in the House and asked a question of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). It pertained to the collapse and the bankruptcy of the Principal Group of companies in Edmonton.
The Minister responded that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was already in the process of assessing matters, and hoped that the depositors would be reimbursed by the CDIC within three weeks of the date of the question. That covers the Principal Savings and Trust Company only of the Principal Group.
I wish to thank the CDIC, through the Minister, for all its efforts in assisting Albertans, and a large number of Edmontonians and constituents of mine from Edmonton East, to deal with the devastating conditions of the loss of their savings, and not of their own making.
I also wish to thank the Minister for the toll-free information line that he established to assist those who were affected. They could call and find out what was happening to their money, if they could get any money back, and what this was all about. People needed assurance, and our Government provided that assurance. I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) showed great sensitivity to the needs of the people when there was a devastation of this magnitude on the financial scale.
The financial services sector in Alberta has been rocked by closures, bankruptcies, and otherwise poor performance within the past few years. Members will recall the closure of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, both in Alberta.
At the present time some credit unions are under a very severe strain and have been restructured because they have also suffered a great deal from the lack of business, and also from the loss of a great deal of business.
The uninitiated may wonder out loud if we in the west really know how to handle our financial affairs. I say of course we do, yes. We do, we can, and we will continue to do that, but

November 3, 1987
Adjournment Debate
this was an extraordinary set of circumstances which affected the regional banks, especially those in the West.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, coming from that great area of Edmonton, regional banks have filled a very important role in Alberta. Usually they are smaller institutions with a flair for serving the unique needs of a particular region.
It seems that recent history has not been kind to regional banks. For instance, the National Energy Program initiated by a federal Government completely devastated Alberta, the energy industry, and ancillary industries. In the construction industry men and women lost their jobs by the tens of thousands. Then there was a world-wide recession which also affected Alberta. Then in January, 1986, the declining world oil price caused a severe drop in the economy of Alberta, and it affected the price of land, buildings, high-rises, homes, and businesses. Alberta's economy, which was so energy dependent, and rightly so, was crushed and it has not been able to bounce back to its former level. Needless to say, many Albertans lost a lot of money. I would like to ensure that their losses were not in vain. I would support any federal initiatives that this Government may take to defend against any similar disasters in the future. It makes no difference whether they occur in Alberta, Saskatchewan, or Nova Scotia.
I feel that there is absolutely no reason why Principal's bankruptcy could not have been avoided. I am wondering whether the federal Government is considering putting in place a system of scrutinizing which would allow it to work with the provinces in order to strengthen regional banks to ensure their viability, and to preserve the very important service that they provide.
The large banks that we have, the Toronto-Dominion, Scotiabank and others with headquarters in eastern Canada have served their needs in the west exceptionally well. But there is one exception. They are not sensitive to the needs of Albertans. This is where the regional banks were able to provide excellent service and where the regional banks had the sensitivity to talk, saying "What can we do and how can we help you? We can give you money".
We in the west need the protection of the federal Government working together with the provincial Government to make sure that the people feel confident in the financial institutions so that the affected companies and the average Albertans will never have to go through this series of bankruptcies again.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS-PRINCIPAL SAVINGS AND TRUST-REIMBURSEMENT OF INVESTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is fitting that you are in the chair tonight. Along with your colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Lesick) many of your constituents have suffered because of this financial loss with Principal Savings and Trust Company. You have shown great concern toward those constituents. That, of course, is continuing in the House this evening.
As Hon. Members know, the Principal Savings and Trust Company, an Alberta supervised trust company within the Principal group was insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. As a result, depositors in this trust company were protected up to the deposit insurance ceiling of $60,000.
The access of insured depositors to their funds has now been restored through an arrangement reached between the CD1C and Metropolitan Trust. Metropolitan Trust began operations on September 14 and has been acting as CDIC's agent in paying out the claims of insured depositors. This arrangement has helped to limit the disruption in financial services to the former depositors of Principal Savings and Trust who had the option of withdrawing their deposits or, if they wished, of redepositing them with Metropolitan Trust.
Though the CDIC is a federal Crown corporation, it should be remembered that there was no direct federal involvement in the Principal group situation since the parent company and all of its affiliates, except for an inactive federally incorporated insurance company, were under the supervision of the Alberta Government. However, the federal Government has placed a high priority on addressing the issues of investor protection and our financial regulation in general, particularly as they relate to federally regulated financial institutions.
The December 18, 1986 policy paper on New Directions for the Financial Sector, which was released by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) paved the way for a number of significant reforms of the regulatory and deposit insurance system. These measures include Bills C-42 and C-56, enacted in June, which increased the supervisory powers of federal regulators and provide the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation with more flexibility in dealing with financially troubled member institutions.
In summary, I would note that the federal Government has seized the initiative in this important sector of the Canadian economy and introduced the comprehensive reform program. Key elements of the program include increasing the financial stability of our financial institutions, providing the regulatory authorities with expanded powers and improving inspection practices. I believe that the proposals represent an effective program that will enhance the soundness and competitiveness of the Canadian financial system. I share the hope with the Hon. Member for Edmonton East that this does not happen again.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS-PRINCIPAL SAVINGS AND TRUST-REIMBURSEMENT OF INVESTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let there be no misunderstanding. The trade deal which Canada has negotiated with the United States does nothing to assist the softwood lumber industry. So far as pulp and paper is concerned, there seems to be no assurances that that industry can breathe more easily without any fear that in the future the United States administration may impose upon it a countervail or at least begin countervail action against it.
November 3, 1987

My question on October 8 concerned why the Government locked in the 1986 softwood lumber memorandum of understanding in the new Canada-U.S. trade agreement. The Minister replied by saying that despite the export tax Canada imposed on the industry, the industry is doing well. She spoke of record production and record profits. She did not, however, tell the whole story.

Many sawmills did close down as a direct result of the 15 per cent export tax. They were producing studding, and they were, it is true, marginal operations. Nevertheless, jobs were lost and communities were affected. Some of those were in my constituency.
The 15 per cent export tax added about $600 million to the cost of Canadian softwood exports. In the first two months after the tax was imposed, the Canadian share of the U.S. softwood lumber market dropped to 28 per cent from 33 per cent. The Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) has said, as reported in an article that appeared recently in a journal on forestry, that the chances of rebuilding the Canadian share of the U.S. market on the basis of price competition are slim.
The industry has done well in some places, thanks to its efficiency, new technology, the availability of good resources, the low Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar and the demand in the United States for a high quality product which we can provide here in Canada. Even if the industry is performing well in certain places now, it still is in a precarious position. What happens if the demand falls, and there are clear indications that housing demands in the United States may fall because of the stock market crash and cautious investment? What happens if at the same time the Canadian dollar, as a result of the Canada-U.S. trade deal, begins to rise to a par with the U.S. dollar?
The answer to the imposition of the 15 per cent tax was originally either to raise the stumpage fees where they were low in Canada or to introduce some sort of provincial levy to take the place of the export tax. In British Columbia, the stumpage fees were raised and they were raised very significantly. Hon. Members should know, however, that despite the fact that stumpage fees were raised, the 15 per cent tax is still there, albeit temporarily. The cost to the industry to produce 1,000 board feet of lumber has gone from $5 to somewhere between $80 and $90.
I said that the tax is still there temporarily. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) was in British Columbia and met with the industry. They thought she would announce that the 15 per cent tax would be lifted immediately because the stumpage fees were going up. Such is not the case. The Minister made it clear that she had to have some discussions in Washington before that could be done and I want Hon. Members to note that.
Adjournment Debate
Meanwhile, the Minister of State for Forestry is having discussions with the Council of Forest Ministers. They have a program designed to exchange the 15 per cent tax for some provincial levies. What has the Minister of State for Forestry said to the Council of Forest Ministers? He has said that on paper the plan looks feasible, it looks acceptable, but he is not sure whether the U.S. lumber industry will not prefer to keep things the way they are. Then he went on to say, however, that the details presented to him will be discussed with the United States of America in two weeks.
It looks to me as if we are beginning to have a new approach to economic decision making in Canada. It looks as if more and more questions about resource revenues will now be decided not in the provincial capitals of this nation, not here in Ottawa, but in Washington, D.C.
I am wondering, and 1 will put it in the form of a question and perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary will find some way to reassure me, if a new pattern is emerging in Canada whereby Canadian resource development policy is really going to have to be ratified in the U.S. If on top of everything else we have unrestricted U.S. investment in our resource economy, if we have decisions about price and marketing made in the U.S., it seems to me as an observer and participant at the very beginning of this important debate on Canada-U.S. trade, that at least a measure of sovereignty is sacrificed. It seems that some of our autonomy is being abandoned. It seems to me that our decisions about the well-being of our economy are going to be delivered into the hands of U.S. officials and politicians.
Nothing in this trade deal helps the softwood lumber industry. I asked in a supplementary question on the same day if the pulp and paper industry was safe. The Minister said I should have no fear, we now have a binational panel. What will it do for us? Will it protect us from unfair U.S. trade laws? Not at all. All it can do is see that the law is equally applied so that Canada does not suffer a greater disadvantage than someone else. Some experts have said we are no better off than we were before, and the Parliamentary Secretary will be interested in what Osier, Hoskin and Harcourt said in a preliminary analysis of the trade deal. Everything is preliminary because we do not have the details.
I conclude on this note. If these new rules had been in effect at the time of last year's U.S. subsidy case against the export of Canadian softwood lumber, the proposed mechanism would not have led to a different result for Canadian exporters than that which occurred. I say that the binational panel is not the answer to the problems of the industry as the Minister suggested in her reply to me.

I will be happy to. First, there is not unfettered, wide-open investment in the resource industry in Canada because of this agreement. It is very obvious to me after listening to him that the Hon. Member has not read the agreement. He has a preliminary opinion from a law firm which says there would be no different decision on the softwood lumber matter. That might very well be true. However, it would be appealed to a bipartisan committee which makes a binding decision. The case is the same as it was in 1983 when the law was fairly applied, except for one thing. The political winds in the U.S. have changed rather dramatically. They have become extremely protectionist. That influenced the decision-making process in the U.S. Department of Commerce. There is no question about that. It was the same case and they did a 180-degree turn from 1983 to 1986. The only difference this time is that we can appeal to a bipartisan committee made up of two Canadians, two Americans and a neutral chairman with a binding decision-making power. If the law was applied wrongly, it can be overturned. It is binding and it is very important.
The pulp and paper industry in Canada has absolutely nothing to fear if it is a fair trader. One of the things that the Hon. Member does not talk about is that Canadian trade laws are basically identical to the American trade laws. It is how they are applied that we are concerned about. We want a fair panel to decide whether they are being applied properly or not. Canadian laws are still in place and they are exactly the same as the American laws. Where we have been having our problems is in the application and that is why this binding dispute settlement mechanism is going to be very important.
As far as softwood lumber is concerned, the stumpage fees and other arrangements being made by the provinces have now been negotiated with the federal Government. We have discussed it and now we are going to present our case to the U.S. The Memorandum of Understanding says very clearly that we must show that we have replaced the 15 per cent tax through provincial initiatives. That is what is going on now in addition to some other anomalies that were in the memorandum of understanding which we are presently trying to straighten out.
Although the tax is being collected at this time it is being placed in a trust fund and will be refunded to the people. The Hon. Member is absolutely right that stumpage fees have gone up and it looks as though a proper replacement has been made.
Therefore, the decision-making on this trade agreement is not in the United States at all. It is a co-operative thing. It is an excellent agreement. The agreement is 33 pages and may take a little time to absorb, but I suggest that the Hon. Member read it because it is very important. I think that when he has read it he will agree that it is a great deal for Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you believe in public opinion polls you believe, as I do, that next to the economy and jobs the greatest concern of Canadians is with the environment. That is why the new Environmental Protection Act which the Government has introduced into Parliament, and which has received first and second reading and is finally before a legislative committee for consideration, is so important.
You know as well as I, Mr. Speaker, that that piece of legislation is only one of a good number of initiatives which the Government has undertaken in the last three years with regard to the environment. The initiatives taken include $40 million contributed by the federal Government and the provinces for the clean-up of the Windermere Basin in Hamilton Harbour as well as the Sydney tar ponds in Nova Scotia which is reputed to be the worst toxic chemical disposal site in eastern Canada.
In addition, the Government has entered into an agreement with the United States Government, Government of the State of New York, and the Government of the Province of Ontario to reduce the toxic chemicals which flow into the Niagara River by 50 per cent by 1996. The initiatives include as well a $2.3 million increase in the budget for pesticide controls and initiatives which have been taken on acid rain. The federal Government is contributing $335 million under agreements with the five eastern provinces to reduce acid rain emissions by one half by 1994.
In addition, new motor vehicle emission standards were introduced in September. An international agreement was reached at Montreal a short time ago on reducing damage to the ozone layer. As well, there will be $1.5 billion invested in the Canada-U.S. North American Waterfowl Management Plan. There is also the $1 million endangered species recovery fund.
Those are all initiatives which the Government has taken. In addition, five new national parks have been designated including the Pacific Rim Park at South Moresby in British Columbia, the Ellesmere Island Park in the Northwest Territories, the Bruce Peninsula Park in Ontario, and the Mingan Islands Park in Quebec. All of these initiatives have been undertaken in the last three years by the Government.
The Environmental Protection Act is another step. It, of course, deals with protecting the environment from new toxic pollution. That Bill is presently in committee and I am looking forward to seeing it passed so that it can help to protect Canadians from toxic chemicals in the future.
That is only one more step, Mr. Speaker. You, I, and the Parliamentary Secretary know that other things should be done as well to clean up the environmental problems which we have now.
November 3, 1987

What we really need on top of all these other things is a superfund like the one that was created in the United States, particularly for the purpose of cleaning up the problem areas in and around the Great Lakes.
There are some 45 industries in Canada that are polluting the Great Lakes. There are some 53 industries in the United States that are polluting the Great Lakes. There are some 10 hazardous waste sites in Canada that are leaking into the Great Lakes and 105 hazardous waste sites in the United States that are leaking into the Great Lakes. There are 32 municipalities in Canada that are polluting the Great Lakes and 81 municipalities in the United States that are polluting the Great Lakes.
We need a clean-up of all those industries, hazardous waste sites and the municipalities, especially the particularly hideous hazardous chemical dumps on the south side of the Niagara River in the United States. They include the Love Canal, High Park, 102nd Street and S Area dumps. All of them are causing enormous pollution.
There is much to be done. The Environmental Protection Bill which is now in committee is one more step in getting under way to solving the problems of the environment and cleaning up pollution. I hope tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will assure us that the Government will be pushing very hard to enact the Environmental Protection Bill into law and will then move on to these other major jobs of cleaning up the polluted areas that already exist in our environment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-INTRODUCTION OF POLLUTION CONTROL LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say how pleased I am that the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has outlined some of the excellent initiatives that this Government has put into place in the three short years we have been in office. I also want to compliment the Member himself for the work he has done in preserving the environment and for his work with the municipalities, having been the Mayor of East York, which is part of the great City of Metropolitan Toronto. I know of his concern and the work he has done.
At the time of the introduction in the House of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act on June 26, 1987, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) also released an enforcement and compliance policy for the new legislation for public comment. The Minister of the Environment invited four non-governmental agencies which specialize in environmental law to critique the compliance policy.
Adjournment Debate
Last month, the Canadian Environmental Law Research Foundation, the Alberta Environmental Law Centre, the West Coast Environmental Law Research Foundation and the Conservation Council of New Brunswick presented their assessments of the enforcement policy at two seminars. The seminars were held in Toronto and in Edmonton, and included participants from industry, provincial governments and public interest groups. These discussions along with the briefs submitted by individuals and industry will assist in finalizing the policy document.
The new Canadian Environmental Protection legislation is the fruit of extensive collaboration among the federal, provincial and territorial governments, as well as industry, organized labour, environmental groups, native and consumer groups. In the months between December, 1986, and March, 1987, Environment Canada officials participated in more than 30 multi-stakeholder meetings throughout the country. It was these consultations, plus 300 letters and briefs, that led to the refinement of the Bill about which the Member was speaking. It recognizes that the protection of the environment is essential to the well-being of Canadians.
We are the first federal Government in Canadian history to put in place comprehensive federal environmental protection legislation. Bill C-74 was debated in this Chamber at second reading for more than 10 hours, during which it was endorsed in principle by all Parties. It has now been passed to committee stage. The Chairman and the committee members have been appointed and I am very pleased that the Hon. Member for York East has been appointed as a member. We will begin our meetings and subsequent clause by clause study, with amendments being considered, and we will be doing that within the next few days.
I can assure this House that this Bill will receive a comprehensive study. The new Act, once passed, provides the basis for eliminating risks to the Canadian environment from toxic chemicals through the closing years of this century and well into the next. We are very pleased with this legislation. Indeed, I would agree with the Hon. Member for York East. We want to pass this legislation as quickly as possible.
